1	This project is written in Piton, a declarative language for agent guidance.
2	
3	- Source of truth: the `.pi` files under `/home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl/spec`. Compiled Markdown is derived output.
4	- Make lasting changes in the Piton source, then run `piton build`; never hand-edit generated artifacts.
5	- Compiled reference documents live under `.claude/reference`. Links between them are lazy: follow one when the work touches what it describes.
6	- Scoped guidance is written to `CLAUDE.md` files placed next to the code they describe.
7	- `piton check` validates the specbase; `piton reach` shows what the entrypoints can see; `piton slice file.pi#Anchor.property` prints just the spec one thing depends on.
8	
9	# Piton Fluency
10	
11	This is a working reference for Piton, the Belay framework bundled with it, the
12	project configuration, the package manager and the tooling. Read it before you
13	read or change a Piton specbase. It is generated from the specification in
14	`spec/` by the GenerateFluencyPrompt skill. Where the compiler behaves
15	differently from the spec, the text below says so, and section 16 lists every
16	known gap.
17	
18	## 1. What Piton is, and why
19	
20	Piton is a declarative, whitespace-structured language for writing agent
21	guidance: skills, agents, commands, scoped instructions and reference
22	documents. Its author calls it a "semi-natural programming language". Prose and
23	structure are both first-class. A value can be a paragraph of plain English or
24	a typed, inherited, composed data structure, and most files mix the two.
25	
26	The founding thesis (`spec/scope/founding-thesis/`) explains the design:
27	
28	- Every programming language is an abstraction over the layer beneath it. Once
29	  an abstraction is accepted, nobody cares how its compiled output is produced,
30	  as long as the output is good. Agentic development is the next step in that
31	  history. In this model the agent is the compiler.
32	- Humans are good at designing coherent systems, not at typing out the latest
33	  accepted abstraction. Piton keeps the describing, constraining and thinking,
34	  and hands the manual labour to the agent.
35	- Prompting an agent session by session produces results that live in one
36	  developer's memory and cannot be traced. AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md and Markdown
37	  skills help, but pure prose decays. It is ambiguous, it gets duplicated, and
38	  it has no tools for reuse. Piton adds imports, inheritance, types and
39	  references to prose, while keeping prose for the things prose says best
40	  ("the button should be blue with contrasting text"). Plain prompting is fine
41	  for a small one-off tool. A sufficiently complex system needs a traceable
42	  artifact of the process itself, not just its output, and more so when
43	  several people work on it.
44	- The real problem is repetition. Much software work is the same patterns
45	  again (CRUD APIs, layouts, navigation bars, modal forms). Functions, classes
46	  and generics are ways of wrapping a problem once it becomes a pattern. The
47	  aim is to keep designing systems and stop typing the patterns: "I never
48	  wanted to write code itself; I wanted to create."
49	- The CNC analogy: G-code replaced the machinist's hand, and CAM then sat on
50	  top of G-code by combining design intent with the machinist's expertise. The
51	  CAM engineer never types G-code but is essential. CNC did not replace most of
52	  the machinist's skill, and two jobs (engineer, machinist) became three (plus
53	  the CAM engineer). The Piton author plays that role for agents.
54	- The stated goal is that you can paste the specification into an agentic
55	  coding tool and get a compiler for Piton and Belay back. This repository is
56	  that experiment. The specification in `spec/` is written in Piton, and the
57	  compiler in `crates/` is judged against it.
58	
59	Core facts:
60	
61	- **There is no runtime.** Piton compiles to data (JSON, YAML, Markdown)
62	  through **renderers**. Frameworks such as Belay add **adapters** on top of
63	  the renderers. There are no functions, no loops, and no conditionals except
64	  the ternary operator. Every value is immutable.
65	- **The `.pi` source is the source of truth.** Compiled Markdown under
66	  `.claude/reference`, `.claude/skills`, `CLAUDE.md` files and so on is derived
67	  output. Make lasting changes in the `.pi` files and rebuild. Never hand-edit
68	  generated artifacts.
69	- A **specbase** is a Piton project: a `piton.config.pi`, a source root
70	  (usually `spec/`), an entry file, and the frameworks and packages it uses.
71	- **Successful compilation shows that the guidance is well-formed. It does not
72	  show that an agent will behave correctly.** Artifact generation is
73	  predictable, but agent behaviour is probabilistic.
74	
75	## 2. Files, whitespace, comments, keywords
76	
77	- Source files use the `.pi` extension. A directory that contains an
78	  `index.pi` is a module (section 7.2).
79	- **Indentation defines structure**, as in Python. Tabs or any number of
80	  spaces are accepted, but one file must be consistent. The canonical style is
81	  4 spaces. `piton format` enforces it, and it cannot be configured.
82	- **Comments** are line-only and start with `//`. There are no block comments.
83	  **A comment has to be on its own line.** After code, `//` is just text, so
84	  `url: https://example.com // note` is the string
85	  `https://example.com // note`. The formatter adds one space after `//` when
86	  there is none and touches nothing else in the comment, so commented-out code
87	  keeps its spacing. To start a value with `//`, escape it:
88	  `\ // \ Just Text`.
89	- **Reserved words** have special meaning:
90	
91	  ```
92	  anchor abstract export from import use as extends pass
93	  this self super
94	  true false null
95	  any simple complex
96	  string number boolean list dictionary
97	  ```
98	
99	  You can't use them as your own keywords (`reserved-keyword`), but **you can
100	  use them as keys**. As keys they are just strings: `null: text`,
101	  `use: text` and `as: text` are ordinary properties.
102	- **Keywords** are all lowercase and may be kebab-case
103	  (`arithmetic-operator`). Users define their own with `as` (section 8.6).
104	- **`pass`** fills the body of an anchor that has no properties of its own. An
105	  anchor always needs something indented under it; `anchor X:` with nothing
106	  under it is `empty-anchor`.
107	
108	  ```piton
109	  anchor Child extends Base:
110	      pass
111	  ```
112	
113	## 3. Declarations and values
114	
115	A file is a sequence of top-level declarations. Top-level names are variables
116	scoped to their file: they are global within the file and invisible outside it
117	unless exported.
118	
119	```piton
120	myVariable: 42
121	export pi: 3.14
122	
123	export anchor MyAnchor:
124	    description: This is my anchor
125	```
126	
127	`key: value` assigns a value, and the space after the colon is required. The
128	value can sit on the same line or be indented on the lines below:
129	
130	```piton
131	sameLine: Hello, World!
132	nextLine:
133	    Hello, World!
134	```
135	
136	Both produce `"Hello, World!"`. The leading indentation belongs to the syntax,
137	not to the string.
138	
139	**A property has to have a value.** A name with nothing after it and nothing
140	indented under it is a compiler error (`empty-value`). If you mean nothing,
141	write `null`. The one exception is a required property in an abstract anchor
142	(`title:: string`); anywhere else a constraint with no value is
143	`missing-value`.
144	
145	### 3.1 Types
146	
147	Piton is loosely typed, with optional constraints.
148	
149	| Type | Notes |
150	| --- | --- |
151	| `string` | Unicode text. Never quoted (section 3.3). |
152	| `number` | One numeric type, a 64-bit IEEE 754 float, with no int/float distinction. |
153	| `boolean` | Lowercase `true` and `false`. |
154	| `null` | Lowercase `null`. It is the only "nothing" value (there is no `undefined`), and `{null == null}` is `true`. |
155	| `list` | An ordered collection. Item types may be mixed unless a constraint says otherwise. |
156	| `dictionary` | Key/value pairs. Keys are strings, and value types may be mixed unless constrained. |
157	| anchor | The one user-defined type (section 8). |
158	
159	- **Simple types** are string, number, boolean and null.
160	- **Complex types** are list, dictionary and anchor.
161	- A **reference** is its own type, produced by `@{}` (section 6.5). It points
162	  at an anchor or a property on one instead of copying it.
163	
164	- **Inference.** An unconstrained variable or property can hold any type,
165	  inferred from how the value looks: `true` is a boolean but `true story` is
166	  a string; `42` and `-42` are numbers but `42 things` is a string; `A + B`
167	  and `This costs $5 + tax` are strings (no braces, no expression); `null` is
168	  null; `"false"` is a string; `${a + b}` is always a string.
169	
170	Every built-in type is described by an anchor that uses the abstract `type`
171	keyword (`spec/scope/language/types/lib/Type.pi`). A `type` anchor provides a
172	`description` (simple or complex) and its `supportedOperators` (a list of
173	operators, or null). Using an operator a type does not list is a compiler
174	error, but the compiler applies the coercion (4.2) and inference rules before
175	it reports one:
176	
177	| Type | Supported operators |
178	| --- | --- |
179	| number | arithmetic `+ - * / %`, comparison `== != < <= > >=` |
180	| string | concatenation `+`, `++`, comparison `== != < <= > >=` |
181	| boolean | logical `&& \|\| !`, `==`, `!=` |
182	| null | `==`, `!=` |
183	| list | merge `+`, `++`, `==`, `!=` |
184	| dictionary | `.`, merge `+`, `++`, `==`, `!=` |
185	| anchor | `.`, `==`, `!=` |
186	| reference | `==`, `!=` |
187	
188	### 3.2 Numbers
189	
190	```piton
191	myInt: 123
192	myFloat: 3.14
193	mySmallFloat: 0.14
194	myBigNumber: 1_200_000.00
195	negative: -5
196	```
197	
198	- **A decimal needs its leading `0`.** `0.14` is a number; `.5` is not a number
199	  (unconstrained, it is the string `".5"`).
200	- `_` may separate digits for readability.
201	- **There is no exponent notation.** `1e3` is not a number (unconstrained, it
202	  is silently the string `"1e3"`, not an error).
203	- A negative number is written with a minus, like `-5`. A list item always has
204	  a space after its dash, so `-5` is a number and `- 5` is a list item.
205	- **The minus is only part of a number.** There's no minus in front of an
206	  expression: `{-price}` is an error. Write `{0 - price}`.
207	- Compiled numbers take their shortest form: `1_200_000.00` becomes `1200000`
208	  and `0.50` becomes `0.5`.
209	
210	### 3.3 Strings and quotes
211	
212	- Strings are not quoted. **Quotes are ordinary characters in a value**, so
213	  `greeting: "Hello"` is the string `"Hello"`, quotes and all, and
214	  `"false"` is a string with quotes in it, never a boolean.
215	- The one exception is inside an expression, where bare words are symbols, so
216	  string operands are written in double quotes: `{"Hello" + name}`. There the
217	  quotes are not part of the string.
218	- In a multi-line block, consecutive lines join with one space. **A blank line
219	  starts a new paragraph**, which compiles to a line break (`\n`). Several
220	  blank lines in a row still count as one.
221	
222	  ```piton
223	  myString:
224	      This broken string is not considered
225	      a line break.
226	
227	      While this *is* a new paragraph because there was a blank line above.
228	  ```
229	
230	  This compiles to
231	  `"This broken string is not considered a line break.\nWhile this *is* a new paragraph because there was a blank line above."`.
232	
233	- **Markdown in a string is plain text.** Piton has no link syntax, so
234	  `[the guide](./guide.md)` and `![A diagram](./diagram.png)` pass through
235	  exactly as written. Nothing resolves, rewrites or checks them, and they are
236	  never an error. The only links Piton makes are `@{}` references.
237	
238	### 3.4 Escaping
239	
240	Escaping works by wrapping. Put backslashes around the special characters,
241	with a space on each side. The spaces are part of the wrapper and are removed:
242	`\ {1 + 2 + 3} \` compiles to the literal `{1 + 2 + 3}`. It is the only way to
243	escape, and even a single character gets wrapped: `\ : \` gives `:`.
244	
245	- **Stacking.** To escape backslashes themselves, use more of them. The
246	  closing wrapper must match the opening one, so anything inside can use fewer:
247	  `\\ \ {x} \ \\` compiles to `\ {x} \`.
248	- **Multi-line escape blocks.** A line holding only backslashes opens a block,
249	  and a line with the same number of backslashes closes it. Everything in
250	  between is kept exactly, line breaks and indentation included. The spec uses
251	  three backslashes (`\\\`) for these.
252	- **Code fences are ordinary text.** A ```` ``` ```` fence does not protect
253	  anything: expressions, comments, list items and keys inside it are still
254	  parsed. So put an escape block inside the fence, the way every example in the
255	  spec does:
256	
257	  ````piton
258	  description:
259	      ```piton
260	      \\\
261	      anchor Example:
262	          value: {1 + 2}
263	      \\\
264	      ```
265	  ````
266	
267	  This keeps the fence and the example exactly as written. Markdown tables
268	  need the same treatment, because otherwise their rows join into one line.
269	
270	**Prose pitfalls.** Each of these silently changes the structure of a string
271	block:
272	
273	- A line that starts `- ` makes a list item, and a line that starts `+ ` or
274	  `++ ` makes a composition line (section 5). A property declared `:: string`
275	  then fails. Escape the start: `\ - \ item`.
276	- A line shaped like `word: text` (`Similarly: ...`, `Inputs: none`, or a
277	  wrapped line that happens to start with `type:`) becomes a dictionary key,
278	  and the block turns into an implicit list. Escape the colon (`\ : \`) or
279	  rewrap the paragraph.
280	- Backticks do not protect anything. `` `{x}` `` is still an expression, and
281	  `` `a + b` `` in a table cell is text only because it has no braces.
282	- An expression in running text changes the value's shape when it evaluates
283	  to a list, dictionary or anchor (section 6.2).
284	
285	Wrapping stops text being parsed as syntax, but it doesn't change the inferred
286	type: `\ false \` is still the boolean `false`. To get the string, write
287	`${false}`.
288	
289	The wrapper is the only way to escape. A backslash that doesn't open a
290	wrapper (a backslash followed by a space) is just a backslash, so `\:` is the
291	two characters `\:`. Write `\ : \` to escape a colon.
292	
293	### 3.5 Lists
294	
295	```piton
296	markdownStyle:
297	    - One
298	    - List
299	    - Item
300	
301	inlineStyle: [This, is, a, list, of, strings]
302	
303	nestedMarkdownList:
304	    - Level 1
305	        - Level 2
306	            - Level 3
307	```
308	
309	`nestedMarkdownList` is `[Level 1, [Level 2, [Level 3]]]`.
310	
311	- **Items cannot be accessed by index.** By design there is no `myList[0]`.
312	  Piton describes things; it does not compute them, and lists exist to be
313	  merged and inherited.
314	- **A list item is never a key**, even with a colon at the end. `- Settings:`
315	  is just the string `"Settings:"`.
316	- **Anything indented under a list item is not part of that item.** It becomes
317	  the next item in the list, so a dictionary indented under an item is its own
318	  item, right after it:
319	
320	  ```piton
321	  repos:
322	      - https://github.com/piton-lang/piton-rs
323	          tag: v1
324	      - https://github.com/piton-lang/other
325	  ```
326	
327	  This compiles to
328	  `["https://github.com/piton-lang/piton-rs", {"tag": "v1"}, "https://github.com/piton-lang/other"]`.
329	  A dictionary that ends up as an item of an explicit list cannot be addressed.
330	
331	### 3.6 Dictionaries
332	
333	A dictionary has one syntax, which is indentation:
334	
335	```piton
336	firstLevel:
337	    secondLevel:
338	        thirdLevel: This is a string
339	```
340	
341	- Dot access works: `{firstLevel.secondLevel.thirdLevel}` gives
342	  `"This is a string"`.
343	- **Valid keys** contain Unicode letters, Unicode digits, `_` and `-`, and
344	  nothing else (no spaces, no dots). Keys are always strings, even when they
345	  look like something else, so `thisIsAKey`, `123`, `foo-bar`, `false` and
346	  `null` are valid keys, while `This is a key` and `a.b` are not.
347	- **A hyphen inside a name is part of the name.** `{config.foo-bar}` reads the
348	  key `foo-bar`. For subtraction, put spaces around the minus: `{a - b}`.
349	- A list indented under a key is that key's value. If the key also has
350	  something above the list, like text or another dictionary, the value becomes
351	  an implicit list (3.7) and the list goes in as one item:
352	
353	  ```piton
354	  plain:
355	      - x
356	      - y
357	  mixed:
358	      text
359	      - x
360	      - y
361	  ```
362	
363	  `plain` is `["x", "y"]`; `mixed` is `["text", ["x", "y"]]`.
364	
365	### 3.7 Implicit lists
366	
367	A block that mixes prose, list items and keys becomes an **implicit list**
368	that keeps the source order:
369	
370	```piton
371	combined:
372	    This is a string
373	
374	    - This
375	    - Is
376	    - A
377	    - List
378	
379	    nestedDictionary:
380	        deeplyNestedDictionary: This is a string
381	```
382	
383	This compiles to
384	`["This is a string", ["This", "Is", "A", "List"], {"nestedDictionary": {"deeplyNestedDictionary": "This is a string"}}]`.
385	
386	- **Keys declared directly in the mixed block stay addressable.**
387	  `{combined.nestedDictionary.deeplyNestedDictionary}` still resolves.
388	- The prose and list elements cannot be addressed, because there is no list
389	  access.
390	- An expression in running text that gives a list, dictionary or anchor also
391	  makes an implicit list (section 6.2).

393	## 4. Variables and type constraints
394	
395	- A variable is declared by naming it at the top level of a file:
396	  `myVariable: 42`.
397	- The file is its scope. `export` makes it visible to other files.
398	- **Inside an expression, a plain name always means a variable from the file
399	  (or something imported), even inside an anchor.** To reach a property on the
400	  anchor you are in, use `this` or `self`:
401	
402	  ```piton
403	  x: top-level
404	
405	  anchor Card:
406	      x: card
407	      fromFile: {x}
408	      fromCard: {this.x}
409	  ```
410	
411	  `Card.fromFile` is `"top-level"` and `Card.fromCard` is `"card"`.
412	- Everything is immutable. There is no compile-time mutability.
413	
414	### 4.1 Constraint syntax
415	
416	A constraint is written `name:: type: value`. **The whitespace after `::` and
417	after `:` is mandatory**, so `myVariable::number:42` is an error
418	(`constraint-spacing`), in blocks as well as at the top level.
419	
420	```piton
421	count:: number: 42
422	tags:: string[]: [foo, bar, baz]
423	config:: dictionary:
424	    a:: number: 1
425	    b:: string: foo
426	a:: complex: [1, 2, 3]
427	c:: simple: 1
428	g:: any: 1
429	h:: any:
430	    - String
431	    - [1, 2, 3]
432	```
433	
434	- `simple` accepts string, number, boolean or null. `complex` accepts list,
435	  dictionary or anchor. `any` accepts anything.
436	- `T[]` is a list of `T`, for any type, including anchor types (`Foo[]`).
437	- `extends Foo[]` (or `extends Foo`) accepts anything that inherits from the
438	  anchor `Foo` (section 8.4). You can use it anywhere, but it is most at home
439	  in abstracts. The spec also uses it on exported lists:
440	  `export ARITHMETIC_OPERATORS:: extends ArithmeticOperator[]: ...`.
441	- An anchor-typed constraint (`f:: Foo: {Foo}`) is satisfied by the anchor or a
442	  copy of it (section 6.1).
443	- A file that names an abstract as a type must import it with
444	  `from ./Foo import Foo`. `use` alone is not enough (section 7.3).
445	
446	### 4.2 Multiple constraints and coercion
447	
448	Coercion is intentionally limited. With several constraints, they are tried
449	**left to right** and the first type the value can validly represent wins.
450	
451	```piton
452	first:: number:: string: 42
453	second:: string:: number: 42
454	written:: string: 1.0
455	evaluated:: string: {1.0}
456	quoted:: boolean:: number:: string: "false"
457	```
458	
459	- `first` is the number `42`; `second` is the string `"42"`.
460	- **A literal keeps its text when coerced to a string.** `written` is
461	  `"1.0"`. An expression is evaluated first and its result is coerced, so
462	  `evaluated` is `"1"`.
463	- `quoted` is the string `"false"`, quotes and all, because quotes are
464	  ordinary characters and `"false"` is not a boolean.
465	- **Booleans and null are never coerced**, to strings or anything else. `flag:: string: false`
466	  is a compiler error (`type-mismatch`), not the string `"false"`. If you want
467	  the string, write `${false}`.
468	- Lists, dictionaries and anchors are never coerced into unrelated types.
469	- If no constraint accepts the value, compilation fails with `type-mismatch`.
470	- These rules are about constraints. Operators such as `+` have their own
471	  rules (section 6.4).
472	
473	### 4.3 Required and optional properties
474	
475	In an abstract anchor:
476	
477	```piton
478	abstract anchor Card:
479	    title:: string
480	    subtitle:: string:: null
481	    footer:: string:: null: null
482	
483	anchor MyCard extends Card:
484	    title: Hello
485	    subtitle: null
486	```
487	
488	- A constraint with no value is **required**. Anything that extends the anchor
489	  has to give it a value (`unimplemented-property` otherwise). Adding `null` to
490	  the constraint lets that value be null, but it still has to be written, so
491	  `title` and `subtitle` are required.
492	- A property with a default value is **optional**. The usual way to write one
493	  is to allow null and default to null, like `footer`. `x:: string:: null: null`
494	  gives `null`. The language server does not complain about a missing
495	  optional property.
496	- **A child can't redeclare a constraint it inherits**, only give it a value.
497	  If `subtitle` is already constrained, `subtitle: Hi` is fine and
498	  `subtitle:: string: Hi` is `redeclared-constraint`.
499	
500	## 5. Composition lines inside blocks
501	
502	**Blocks are built from top to bottom. A line that starts with `+` or `++`
503	takes everything above it and combines it with that line's value**, using the
504	operator of the same name (section 6.4).
505	
506	```piton
507	anchor BaseAnchor:
508	    items:
509	        - A
510	        - B
511	        - C
512	
513	anchor ChildAnchor extends BaseAnchor:
514	    items:
515	        + {super.items}
516	        - D
517	        - E
518	        - F
519	```
520	
521	`ChildAnchor.items` is `[A, B, C, D, E, F]`: the block starts empty, the `+`
522	brings in `super.items`, then D, E and F are added. Without the `+`
523	(`- {super.items}`) the result is `[[A, B, C], D, E, F]`.
524	
525	- On lists, `+` merges and **removes duplicates, keeping the last
526	  occurrence**. Items `A, B, C, D` followed by `+ {super.items}` give
527	  `[D, A, B, C]`.
528	- On lists, `++` keeps everything: items `A, B, C, D` followed by
529	  `++ {super.items}` give `[A, B, C, D, A, B, C]`.
530	- On dictionaries, `+` is a shallow merge and `++` a deep merge.
531	- **On strings, `+` joins with nothing in between and `++` joins with a line
532	  break:**
533	
534	  ```piton
535	  anchor Base:
536	      d: Base text.
537	
538	  anchor Plus extends Base:
539	      d:
540	          Child text.
541	          + {super.d}
542	
543	  anchor DoublePlus extends Base:
544	      d:
545	          Child text.
546	          ++ {super.d}
547	  ```
548	
549	  `Plus.d` is `"Child text.Base text."` and `DoublePlus.d` is
550	  `"Child text.\nBase text."`.
551	- A block holding only `+ {x}` is the same as `{x}`.
552	- To put inherited prose in front with a space, interpolate instead:
553	  `${super.description} and more from the child.`
554	
555	## 6. Expressions
556	
557	**Nothing is evaluated unless it is in braces.** `a + b` is the string
558	`"a + b"`, and `{a + b}` is `3` when `a` is 1 and `b` is 2. The braces keep the
559	compiler simple, and they mean an unrecognized word never silently falls back
560	to being a string.
561	
562	- Inside the braces, **bare words are symbols**. Quote string operands:
563	  `{2 + "Hello"}` gives `"2Hello"`. An unknown name is `unresolved-symbol`.
564	  List literals inside braces follow the same rule: `{["A", "B"] + ["C"]}`.
565	- **Keep the whole expression inside the braces.** `{this.flag && false}`
566	  evaluates; `{this.flag} && false` is text around an expression.
567	- **Braces that don't hold a valid expression are an error**, and so is an
568	  empty `{}` or `${}`. To write braces as text, escape them: `\ {1 +} \`.
569	- **Forward references resolve.** Unresolved references are errors, and so are
570	  cyclic values: `A: {B}` together with `B: {A}` fails with `cyclic-value`.
571	- Collections are copied by value:
572	
573	  ```piton
574	  myList: [1, 2, 3]
575	  myDictionary:
576	      list: {myList}
577	  newList: {myDictionary.list + [4, 5, 6]}
578	  ```
579	
580	  `newList` is `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]`.
581	- **Anchors are copied too, but the copy still knows which anchor it is.** If
582	  `x` is `{Foo}`, then `{x == Foo}` is `true`, `${x}` is `"Foo"`, and `x`
583	  passes a `Foo` type constraint. The output is still a copy of Foo's content.
584	  For a link instead of a copy, use `@{Foo}`.
585	
586	### 6.1 The four expression forms
587	
588	| Form | Name | Result |
589	| --- | --- | --- |
590	| `{expr}` | Standard | The intrinsic value with its type preserved. An anchor serializes as its resolved content (a copy that keeps its identity). |
591	| `${expr}` | String | Converts the result to a string. |
592	| `#{expr}` | Numeric | Converts the result to a number. |
593	| `@{expr}` | Reference | A reference to an anchor or a property on one. Renders as a link or path, never as the content. |
594	
595	Use `@{X}` to point at another document, `{X}` to embed a copy of it, and
596	`${X}` to mention it by name.
597	
598	### 6.2 Expressions in text
599	
600	If the whole value is one expression (`total: {a + b}`), it keeps its type. If
601	there is other text around it:
602	
603	- `${x}` turns the result into a string, so the whole value is a string.
604	- `{x}` with a simple value drops it into the text: `Total: {a + b}` is
605	  `"Total: 3"`.
606	- `{x}` with a list, dictionary or anchor copies it in and **turns the
607	  property into an implicit list**. `See {Foo} for details` becomes a list of
608	  `"See"`, a copy of Foo, and `"for details"`.
609	- `@{x}` puts in a reference, which ends up as a link or a path.
610	
611	### 6.3 Conversions
612	
613	`${}` (string):
614	
615	- A string is returned unchanged. A number becomes its text form. A boolean
616	  becomes `true` or `false`. Null becomes `null`.
617	- An anchor becomes its name as written in the source: `${Child}` gives
618	  `"Child"`, and `${self}` gives the name of the current most-derived anchor.
619	  It is not turned into a title.
620	- A named list or dictionary becomes its name: `Anchor.propertyName`, or just
621	  the variable name at the top of a file. So if `tags` is a top-level list,
622	  `${tags}` is `"tags"`.
623	- A list or dictionary with no name (`${[1, 2]}`) is `no-string-form`.
624	- **`${}` never pulls in the contents** of a list, dictionary or anchor, only
625	  its name. For the contents use `{x}`; for a link use `@{x}`. In
626	  `Metadata.pi`:
627	
628	  ```piton
629	  export anchor Metadata:
630	      name: Piton
631	      version:: string: 1.0
632	
633	  export byName: Information about Piton ${Metadata}
634	  export byValue: Information about Piton {Metadata}
635	  export byLink: Information about Piton @{Metadata}
636	  ```
637	
638	  `byName` is `"Information about Piton Metadata"`, `byValue` is
639	  `["Information about Piton", {"name": "Piton", "version": "1.0"}]`, and
640	  `byLink` is `"Information about Piton ./Metadata.json:Metadata"` (in
641	  Markdown, `[Metadata](./Metadata.md#metadata)`).
642	- The result is never re-parsed as source.
643	- In structured output the value stays a string; whatever escaping the output
644	  format needs is applied when it is serialized.
645	
646	`#{}` (numeric):
647	
648	- A number is returned unchanged. A string converts only if the **entire**
649	  string is a valid Piton numeric literal: `#{"42"}` gives `42`. It is never
650	  evaluated as an expression.
651	- Booleans, null, collections and anchors are rejected (`not-a-number`).
652	- The result is a number you can keep computing with. In structured output it
653	  stays numeric; it becomes text only when the output format needs text.
654	
655	### 6.4 Operators
656	
657	| Group | Operators | Rules |
658	| --- | --- | --- |
659	| Access | `.` | Property access on dictionaries and anchors. |
660	| Arithmetic | `+ - * / %` | Numbers only. Division or modulo by zero is an error. `%` keeps the sign of the left side: `{-7 % 3}` is `-1`. |
661	| Comparison | `== != < <= > >=` | The result is a boolean. `==` and `!=` work on every type (see below). `< <= > >=` work on numbers and on strings (by Unicode code point); anything else, or a number against a string, is an error. |
662	| Logical | `&& \|\| !` | Booleans only. **There is no truthiness**; anything else is `invalid-operand`. **No short-circuiting**: both sides are always evaluated and must be booleans, so `{true \|\| 5}` and `{false && 1 / 0 == 1}` are both errors. |
663	| Conditional | `cond ? a : b` | The condition must be a boolean (`invalid-condition`). Only the selected branch is evaluated. Chainable in either slot. |
664	| Concatenation / merge | `+` | Dispatches on the operand types (table below). |
665	| Duplicate merge | `++` | Lists: joined in order, duplicates kept. Dictionaries: deep merge (nested dictionaries on both sides are merged all the way down; otherwise the right side wins). Strings: joined with a line break. |
666	
667	**`+` dispatch:**
668	
669	| Left | Right | Operation |
670	| --- | --- | --- |
671	| number | number | addition |
672	| string | simple | concatenation |
673	| simple | string | concatenation |
674	| string | list, dictionary or anchor | implicit list |
675	| list, dictionary or anchor | string | implicit list |
676	| list | list | merge: joined in order, duplicates removed, last occurrence kept |
677	| dictionary | dictionary | shallow merge: keys from both, right side wins |
678	| anything else | | compiler error |
679	
680	- Concatenation stringifies the non-string side by the `${}` rules:
681	  `{2 + "Hello"}` is `"2Hello"` and `{"Enabled: " + true}` is
682	  `"Enabled: true"`.
683	- A list, dictionary or anchor is never stringified by `+`. If `tags` is
684	  `[a, b]`, `{"Tags: " + tags}` is `["Tags: ", ["a", "b"]]`. Use `${tags}` if
685	  you want the name.
686	- `{["A", "B", "C", "D"] + ["A", "B", "C"]}` is `[D, A, B, C]`;
687	  `{["A", "B", "C", "D"] ++ ["A", "B", "C"]}` is `[A, B, C, D, A, B, C]`.
688	- `{1 + true}`, `{null + 1}` and `{1 ++ 2}` are errors (`invalid-operand`).
689	
690	**Equality:** lists and dictionaries are equal if everything inside them is
691	equal. Anchors are equal only if they are the same anchor, and references only
692	if they point at the same thing.
693	
694	**Precedence** (higher rows go first; the same row goes left to right, except
695	the ternary, which goes right to left; parentheses change the order):
696	
697	| Precedence | Operators |
698	| --- | --- |
699	| 1 (highest) | `.` |
700	| 2 | `!` |
701	| 3 | `*` `/` `%` |
702	| 4 | `+` `-` `++` |
703	| 5 | `<` `<=` `>` `>=` |
704	| 6 | `==` `!=` |
705	| 7 | `&&` |
706	| 8 | `\|\|` |
707	| 9 (lowest) | `? :` |
708	
709	So `{1 + 2 == 3 && !false}` is `{((1 + 2) == 3) && (!false)}`, and
710	`{a ? b : c ? d : e}` is `{a ? b : (c ? d : e)}`.
711	
712	**Control flow:** the ternary is the only conditional, and the only operator
713	that evaluates just one side. There are no loops and no functions.
714	
715	**Declaration operators:** `:` (assignment) and `::` (type annotation) are
716	documented as operators in `spec/scope/language/operators/declaration/`
717	(`DeclarationOperators`), but they are not expression operators: they aren't in
718	`allOperators`, the precedence table, or any type's `supportedOperators`.
719	
720	**Why `+` and `++`:** on lists, `+` behaves like a set (duplicates removed,
721	last kept) and `++` like a list (duplicates kept). The spec explains this in
722	`ConcatenationOperators.setsAndLists`.
723	
724	### 6.5 References `@{}`
725	
726	- The expression must identify an anchor or **a property on one**
727	  (`@{Button}`, `@{Button.color}`). Anything else is `invalid-reference`.
728	  **A plain list or dictionary at the top of a file can't be referenced**; to
729	  link to it, put it in an anchor.
730	- The referenced anchor joins the compilation dependency graph (for a
731	  property, the anchor it is on), so it gets compiled and emitted.
732	- References are resolved separately for each output target, through the
733	  renderer or the framework adapter on top of it. If a target cannot represent
734	  a reference, that is an error. A reference never silently becomes an
735	  embedded copy or a plain name.
736	- References compare with `==` and `!=`: equal if they point at the same
737	  thing.
738	- How each renderer writes one:
739	
740	  | Renderer | Reference to `Button` | Reference to `Button.color` |
741	  | --- | --- | --- |
742	  | JSON | `"./Button.json:Button"` | `"./Button.json:Button.color"` |
743	  | YAML | `./Button.yaml:Button` | `./Button.yaml:Button.color` |
744	  | Markdown | `[Button](./Button.md#button)` | `[Button.color](./Button.md#color)` |
745	
746	  JSON and YAML write the path to the other output file (relative to this
747	  one), a colon, and the dot path. Markdown writes a relative link with the
748	  anchor's name (or `Anchor.property`) as the link text, and a fragment for the
749	  specific anchor or property heading. The link is **lazy**: the content is
750	  not inlined, and an agent follows it only when the work touches what it
751	  describes.
752	- A Markdown link you write yourself (`[Button](./Button.md)`) is plain text,
753	  not a reference. Only `@{...}` is resolved and checked.

755	## 7. Modules and reuse
756	
757	### 7.1 Export and import
758	
759	```piton
760	export pi: 3.14
761	myVariable: 42
762	export anchor MyAnchor:
763	    description: This is my anchor
764	```
765	
766	`myVariable` is not exported, so no other file can import it.
767	
768	```piton
769	from ./FirstFile import pi, MyAnchor
770	from ./FirstFile import pi SliceOf, MyAnchor MyAliasedAnchor
771	from /subdir/subdir/file import AnAnchor
772	from ./path/to/directory import MyAnchor
773	from .. import Something
774	from my-package import MyAnchor
775	from @piton/belay import ClaudeCodeAdapter
776	from ./file import
777	    FirstThing,
778	    SecondThing,
779	    ThirdThing
780	```
781	
782	- Paths are relative to the current file. A path that starts with `/` is
783	  relative to the `root` in `piton.config.pi`.
784	- **The `.pi` extension is optional**, and `piton format` removes it.
785	- A bare `.` or `..` points at the `index.pi` in that directory. A directory
786	  path resolves to its `index.pi`.
787	- Only exported names can be imported (`unresolved-export`). A missing module
788	  is `unresolved-module`.
789	- Aliasing is `Name Alias`, with no `as`. After aliasing, only the alias is in
790	  scope (`pi` above is available only as `SliceOf`).
791	- `export Name` on its own line re-exports something already declared or
792	  imported.
793	- **Circular imports are allowed.** Mutually referencing values are fine as
794	  long as every value settles:
795	
796	  ```piton
797	  anchor A:
798	      description: This anchor talks about ${B}
799	
800	  anchor B:
801	      description: This anchor talks about ${A}
802	  ```
803	
804	  This works because both settle to strings (the anchor names). `A: {B}` with
805	  `B: {A}` cannot resolve, so it fails. The only cycles that are errors are
806	  ones that can't resolve and an anchor that ends up extending itself.
807	
808	### 7.2 Index files and re-export
809	
810	An `index.pi` file exposes a directory as a module:
811	
812	```piton
813	from ./MyAnchor import MyAnchor
814	export MyAnchor
815	```
816	
817	The shorter forms:
818	
819	```piton
820	from ./MyAnchor export MyAnchor
821	from ./MyAnchor export *
822	from ./MyAnchor export MyAnchor MyAliasedAnchor, MyOtherAnchor MyOtherAliasedAnchor
823	```
824	
825	**Importing a name into an index does not re-export it.** When an index uses
826	`import`, consumers must import leaf anchors from their own files, or the
827	index must `export` them.
828	
829	### 7.3 `use`
830	
831	`use` brings the **user-defined keywords** a module exports into scope, and
832	nothing else. `from ... import` never brings keywords.
833	
834	```piton
835	use ./CustomKeywords
836	
837	my-custom-keyword Wow:
838	    description: amazing
839	```
840	
841	- Valid forms include `use ./CustomKeywords`, `use .`, `use ../cli`,
842	  `use my-package`, `use my-package/MyAnchor` and `use @piton/belay`.
843	- A file that declares with a keyword *and* names its abstract as a type needs
844	  both lines: `use ./Foo` and `from ./Foo import Foo`.
845	- Using a keyword without `use` gives `unknown-keyword`.
846	
847	### 7.4 Formatting of imports
848	
849	`piton format` sorts the imports: in each run of import lines, the `use`
850	lines come first, then the `from` lines, each sorted by path, and the names in
851	each line are sorted too. A blank line keeps two runs apart. It breaks an
852	import or `from ... export` line across lines when it has more than 2 items or
853	runs past 80 columns, and drops the `.pi` extension from paths. You can write
854	those line breaks yourself on either kind of line.

856	## 8. Anchors
857	
858	An anchor is a named structural declaration that can take part in
859	inheritance, typing, exports and composition. It is the core building block of
860	Piton, something like a class that is never instantiated. An *object* is a
861	value. An *anchor* is a declaration.
862	
863	```piton
864	export anchor MyFirstAnchor:
865	    whatIsAnAnchor:
866	        An anchor is a kind of object or document that is structured via
867	        properties and values.
868	    listTypes:
869	        - List types
870	        - are supported.
871	    numberTypes: {3.14 - 3.14}
872	    booleanTypes: true
873	    nullType: null
874	    booleanOperatorsAnd: {this.booleanTypes && false}
875	    booleanOperatorsOr: {this.booleanTypes || false}
876	```
877	
878	Compiled to JSON, an anchor becomes an object of its resolved properties
879	(`numberTypes` is `0`, `booleanOperatorsAnd` is `false`,
880	`booleanOperatorsOr` is `true`). Valid anchor keys follow the dictionary rules.
881	
882	### 8.1 Structural inheritance
883	
884	`anchor Child extends A, B:` copies the properties of every base and then
885	applies the child's own. On a collision, **the right-most base wins, and the
886	child beats every base.** Type constraints from bases follow the same rule
887	(abstracts have their own, 8.4). This is structural inheritance, not
888	polymorphism.
889	
890	```piton
891	anchor FirstBaseAnchor:
892	    firstBaseAnchorProperty: Hello from the First Base Anchor
893	    description: Description from FirstBaseAnchor
894	
895	anchor SecondBaseAnchor:
896	    secondBaseAnchorProperty: Hello from the Second Base Anchor
897	    description: Description from SecondBaseAnchor
898	
899	anchor ChildAnchor extends FirstBaseAnchor, SecondBaseAnchor:
900	    childAnchorProperty: Hello from Child Anchor
901	```
902	
903	`ChildAnchor.description` is `"Description from SecondBaseAnchor"`.
904	
905	- An anchor can't extend itself, directly or through others
906	  (`inheritance-cycle`). Extending something that is not an anchor is
907	  `invalid-base`; an unknown base is `unresolved-base`.
908	- A child can't redeclare an inherited constraint (4.3).
909	
910	### 8.2 `super`
911	
912	`super` is everything the anchor inherits, merged the same way as property
913	inheritance: left to right, last in line wins. **So if the last base doesn't
914	have the property, `super` still finds it on an earlier one.**
915	
916	```piton
917	anchor Left:
918	    d: from-left
919	
920	anchor Right:
921	    other: x
922	
923	anchor Child extends Left, Right:
924	    d: ${super.d} plus child
925	```
926	
927	`Child.d` is `"from-left plus child"`. If no base has the property, that is a
928	compiler error. Use `${super.x}` to extend prose, and a `+ {super.items}`
929	line to extend a list (section 5).
930	
931	### 8.3 `self` and `this`
932	
933	- **`self`** means the most-derived anchor, and it travels down the hierarchy.
934	  When a base writes `${self.name}`, a child compiled from it shows the child's
935	  name.
936	- **`this`** is pinned to the anchor that lexically contains the expression.
937	  When a base writes `${this.name}`, it always shows the base's own value,
938	  including in anchors that inherit it. When a child overrides the property,
939	  the override's own `this` refers to the child.
940	
941	```piton
942	anchor Base:
943	    name: Base Anchor
944	    baseDescription: This is ${this.name}
945	
946	anchor MidChild extends Base:
947	    name: MidChild Anchor
948	    baseDescription: Override on baseDescription ${this.name}
949	    childDescription: This is ${self.name}
950	
951	anchor FinalChild extends MidChild:
952	    name: FinalChild Anchor
953	```
954	
955	`FinalChild` is `{"name": "FinalChild Anchor", "baseDescription": "Override on baseDescription MidChild Anchor", "childDescription": "This is FinalChild Anchor"}`.
956	
957	- `self` only travels through inheritance. Reading a property from another
958	  anchor gives that anchor's value, with `self` being that anchor:
959	
960	  ```piton
961	  anchor Precedence:
962	      note: ${self} rules apply
963	
964	  anchor Addition:
965	      copied: ${Precedence.note}
966	  ```
967	
968	  `Addition.copied` is `"Precedence rules apply"`.
969	- `this` and `self` always mean an anchor, never a dictionary. Even inside a
970	  nested dictionary, they mean the anchor it is in.
971	- Using `self`, `this` or `super` outside an anchor is an error
972	  (`invalid-self`, `invalid-this`, `invalid-super`).
973	
974	### 8.4 Abstract anchors
975	
976	```piton
977	abstract anchor Construct:
978	    description:: string
979	    prompt:: string
980	
981	abstract anchor Skill extends Construct as skill:
982	    useWhen:: string
983	
984	skill Review:
985	    description: Reviews code
986	    prompt: Review the diff
987	    useWhen: Asked for a review
988	```
989	
990	- An abstract anchor defines a shape without necessarily providing values. It
991	  **never compiles on its own** and produces no output. A concrete anchor that
992	  extends it *implements* it and must give every required property a value
993	  (`unimplemented-property`). A property with a default is optional (4.3).
994	- If nothing implements an abstract, you get a warning
995	  (`unimplemented-abstract`), unless it's exported, since another file or
996	  project may implement it.
997	- An abstract may extend another abstract. The implementer has to fill in the
998	  required properties from the whole chain.
999	- **An anchor can implement more than one abstract**, even ones that share a
1000	  base, and it can extend concrete anchors as well. If two abstracts constrain
1001	  the same property to types that don't overlap at all (say string and
1002	  number), that is `conflicting-abstracts`. If they overlap, the right-most
1003	  one wins. Constraints from concrete bases follow normal inheritance.
1004	- Good practice is to export an abstract with a keyword. The keyword's anchor
1005	  always goes last in the chain, so it wins (8.6).
1006	- All the special constraints (`simple`, `complex`, `any`, `[]`, `extends`)
1007	  work inside abstracts.
1008	- **Anchor-type constraints:**
1009	
1010	  ```piton
1011	  abstract anchor A:
1012	      description:: string
1013	
1014	  abstract anchor B extends A:
1015	      name:: string
1016	
1017	  abstract anchor C:
1018	      listOfA:: A[]
1019	      listOfB:: B[]
1020	      listOfExtendsA:: extends A[]
1021	  ```
1022	
1023	  A plain anchor type only matches anchors that **directly implement** it, so
1024	  `listOfA` takes anchors implementing `A`, and something implementing `B`
1025	  does not fit even though `B extends A`. When an anchor has several
1026	  abstracts, the one that counts is the winning one: the keyword's abstract,
1027	  or else the right-most. `extends A[]` accepts any **concrete** anchor whose
1028	  inheritance chain includes `A`, so implementers of `A` or `B` both fit.
1029	- Extra properties a concrete anchor adds beyond the abstract's shape are
1030	  kept. Belay relies on this: extra properties on a construct are serialized
1031	  into the generated guidance.
1032	
1033	### 8.5 Value-less declarations
1034	
1035	`name:: type` with no value is only allowed inside an abstract anchor, where
1036	it declares a required property. Anywhere else it is `missing-value`, and an
1037	empty `name:` anywhere is `empty-value`.
1038	
1039	### 8.6 User-defined keywords
1040	
1041	`as` gives an anchor a keyword alias. Declaring with the keyword is syntactic
1042	sugar for `extends`:
1043	
1044	```piton
1045	anchor MyAnchor as my-anchor:
1046	    description: This is a description of my anchor
1047	
1048	anchor OtherBase:
1049	    description: Other Base
1050	
1051	my-anchor ChildAnchor extends OtherBase:
1052	    description:
1053	        ${super.description}
1054	        My additional description
1055	```
1056	
1057	- `my-anchor ChildAnchor:` is exactly `anchor ChildAnchor extends MyAnchor:`.
1058	  Keywords exist to mark certain base anchors as the fundamental units of a
1059	  design.
1060	- `my-anchor ChildAnchor extends OtherBase:` is exactly
1061	  `anchor ChildAnchor extends OtherBase, MyAnchor:`. **The keyword's anchor is
1062	  the last base, so it wins collisions** with what is in `extends`. Here
1063	  `ChildAnchor.description` starts with "This is a description of my anchor".
1064	- Only one keyword per anchor, but `extends` can add more bases.
1065	- A keyword can be built on another keyword:
1066	  `export abstract operator ArithmeticOperator as arithmetic-operator:`
1067	  declares with the `operator` keyword and defines `arithmetic-operator`.
1068	- To declare with a keyword, a file must `use` the module that exports it.
1069	- A reserved word can't be a keyword (`reserved-keyword`).
1070	
1071	## 9. Compilation model
1072	
1073	- **`piton compile <file>`** produces one object with **one key per export**.
1074	  Anything not exported is left out, and so are abstract anchors. (The JSON
1075	  examples in the spec skip the export wrapper to stay short.)
1076	- **`piton build`** compiles the project. Everything exported from the entry
1077	  file is compiled, whether or not anything uses it, plus anything those
1078	  exports reference, so the links have somewhere to go. Everything else is
1079	  left out, and abstract anchors never compile.
1080	- **Renderers** decide the format: `json` (default), `yaml` or `markdown`.
1081	  Frameworks add adapters on top; Belay's adapters build on the Markdown
1082	  renderer.
1083	- **Markdown serialization** (used by the Markdown renderer and Belay; the
1084	  worked examples are in `spec/scope/belay/Compilation.pi`,
1085	  `MarkdownSerialization`):
1086	  - Anchor and property names become word-separated title headings.
1087	    `myProperty` becomes `My Property`, `t1` becomes `T 1`, and runs of
1088	    capitals are not split (`whatIsAType` becomes `What Is AType`). Heading
1089	    depth follows nesting, and bold labels (`**G**`) take over past level 6.
1090	  - **Every property of an anchor gets a heading**, even one holding a single
1091	    `false` or `42`, with the value under it.
1092	  - A **pure dictionary** is one whose every value is a simple value (string,
1093	    number, boolean, null) or another pure dictionary: no lists and no mixed
1094	    content anywhere inside. It is written as-is, indentation-structured,
1095	    inside a code fence, and its keys don't become headings, including when
1096	    it's embedded in mixed content.
1097	  - A dictionary that isn't pure, and any mixed content, gets a heading per
1098	    key instead.
1099	  - **Strings count as simple values, even long prose**, so a dictionary whose
1100	    values are all prose is fenced. To get a heading per key, start the block
1101	    with a line of prose before the keys, or make at least one value a list.
1102	  - Primitives become their text form (`false`, `42`, `null`).
1103	  - Explicit lists become Markdown lists with nested indentation.
1104	  - Mixed lists keep the order of their prose and structure.
1105	  - `{Other}` is serialized as a copy of the anchor's content. Only `@{Other}`
1106	    becomes a link.
1107	- **Interpolation boundary:** Piton evaluates expressions, and the output mode
1108	  decides how the results appear. The distinction between intrinsic values,
1109	  strings and references is preserved. Reference identity is never inferred
1110	  from a display heading.

1112	## 10. Project configuration (`piton.config.pi`)
1113	
1114	The compiler reads `piton.config.pi` from the working directory. The
1115	configuration anchors come from the bundled `@piton/config`. The file exports
1116	its main `piton-config` anchor, and the language server treats it as a project
1117	config, not as an ordinary source file.
1118	
1119	```piton
1120	use @piton/config
1121	use @piton/belay
1122	use @piton/packaging
1123	
1124	from @piton/belay import ClaudeCodeAdapter
1125	
1126	export piton-config Config:
1127	    root: ./spec
1128	    entry: ./spec/index.pi
1129	    output: ./dist
1130	    renderer: json
1131	
1132	    frameworks:
1133	        - {BelayConfiguration}
1134	
1135	    packages:
1136	        - {MyPackage}
1137	
1138	    dependencies:
1139	        - https://github.com/org/repo
1140	            tag: 1.0
1141	
1142	belay-config BelayConfiguration:
1143	    codeRoot: ./src
1144	    shapeRoot: ./spec/shape
1145	
1146	    adapters:
1147	        - {ClaudeCodeAdapter}
1148	
1149	piton-package MyPackage:
1150	    name: my-package
1151	    root: ./spec/pkg
1152	```
1153	
1154	| Field | Meaning |

1155	| --- | --- |
1156	| `root` | Required. The source root; `/`-imports resolve from it. |
1157	| `entry` | Optional. Defaults to `index.pi` inside `root`; if that doesn't exist, it's an error. |
1158	| `output` | Optional. Where `piton build` writes renderer output. Defaults to `./dist`. With a framework, the renderer output is only written when `output` or `renderer` is set. |
1159	| `renderer` | Optional. `json`, `yaml` or `markdown`. Defaults to `json`. |
1160	| `frameworks` | Optional. Framework configurations to turn on (Belay's `belay-config`). |
1161	| `packages` | Optional. The packages this repository **offers** to other projects (section 12). |
1162	| `dependencies` | Optional. The packages this project installs (section 12). |
1163	
1164	What the bundled packages define:
1165	
1166	```piton
1167	export abstract anchor PitonConfig as piton-config:
1168	    root:: string
1169	    entry:: string:: null: null
1170	    output:: string:: null: null
1171	    renderer:: string:: null: null
1172	    frameworks:: list:: null: null
1173	    packages:: list:: null: null
1174	    dependencies:: list:: null: null
1175	
1176	export abstract anchor FrameworkConfig as framework-config:
1177	    pass
1178	
1179	export abstract anchor PitonPackage as piton-package:
1180	    name:: string:: null: null
1181	    root:: string
1182	    dependencies:: list:: null: null
1183	```
1184	
1185	(`PitonConfig` and `FrameworkConfig` come from `@piton/config`, `PitonPackage`
1186	from `@piton/packaging`, and `BelayConfig`, keyword `belay-config`, from
1187	`@piton/belay`; see 11.1.)
1188	
1189	**Frameworks.** A framework extends what the compiler outputs by adding
1190	adapters on top of the renderers. Belay is the only framework today. **You can
1191	use and import a bundled framework's keywords and modules whether or not it is
1192	registered**, and each file still has to `use` or `import` what it needs;
1193	registration is not an implicit import. **Registering the framework in
1194	`frameworks:` is what turns on its output.**
1195	
1196	Configuration diagnostics include `missing-config`, `unknown-config-key`,
1197	`unknown-framework`, `unknown-adapter`, `invalid-adapter`,
1198	`package-without-root`, `invalid-package-name` and `multiple-pins`.

1200	## 11. Belay: the agentic framework
1201	
1202	Belay is bundled as `@piton/belay`. It gives Piton a vocabulary for agents and
1203	compiles it into the artifacts that agentic coding tools read. The division of
1204	labour:
1205	
1206	- **Piton** handles parsing, evaluation, imports, exports, inheritance,
1207	  reachability and the renderers.
1208	- **Belay** adds the constructs and the adapters that turn them into files for
1209	  each platform.
1210	- The **consuming platform** executes the result. Successful compilation is
1211	  not proof of correct agent execution.
1212	
1213	Besides the four constructs, Belay provides `belay-config`, the adapters and
1214	the special imports.
1215	
1216	Source authority: lasting changes go into the Piton source. Generated guidance
1217	is derived from the resolved source and configuration, and implementation is
1218	assessed against the specification. The compiler loads the four constructs and
1219	the three adapters from the spec's own `.pi` files
1220	(`spec/scope/belay/anchors/`, `spec/scope/belay/adapters/`), so the compiler
1221	and the spec can't disagree: changing `Skill.pi` changes the framework.
1222	
1223	### 11.1 Configuration
1224	
1225	A project turns on Belay by listing a `belay-config` anchor under
1226	`frameworks`:
1227	
1228	| Field | Meaning |

1313	
1314	- **Emission.** Belay emits only what the build emits: the entry file's
1315	  exports and anything they reference.

1317	  `referenceRoot`, **one Markdown file per source module**, keeping the
1318	  module's path under `root`. Each anchor is a heading in its module's file.

1380	Rules for every adapter:
1381	
1382	- **Pipeline:** take the emitted, validated constructs from Piton, build one
1383	  output plan per adapter, resolve instruction placement and reference
1384	  destinations, check shared paths and cross-discovery across the whole plan,
1385	  serialize, validate links, metadata, names and output ownership, then write.
1386	- Every adapter carries `documentationChecked` (currently `2026-09-21`): the
1387	  date its target's documentation was last checked, recorded in the
1388	  manifest's `targets`.
1389	- Constructs are consumed **after** imports and inheritance resolve. Each of
1390	  the four constructs is mapped explicitly for each target.
1391	- An adapter distinguishes native support, translation and unsupported
1392	  behaviour, and fails with an actionable diagnostic when required behaviour
1393	  can't be represented.
1394	- Model and permission settings are applied **only when configured
1395	  explicitly**. Absent settings are omitted so native defaults apply. Native
1396	  options are validated against the target platform version, and role,
1397	  prompt and other prose never get copied into metadata fields.
1398	- **A prompt that requests restraint is not an enforced restriction.** An
1399	  adapter claims enforcement only for controls the platform applies, and never
1400	  translates permissions in a way that silently widens access. Claude's
1401	  `allowed-tools` and subagent `tools` serve different purposes; neither is a
1402	  portable sandbox. Requesting an enforced restriction the adapter can't
1403	  represent is a diagnostic.
1404	- An adapter never silently turns an agent into a skill, or a command into an
1405	  automatically invoked skill, when that changes how it activates.
1406	- Names are normalized before planning, and commands keep the `x-` prefix
1407	  after normalization. Collisions are errors (`name-collision`,
1408	  `output-collision`) unless the artifacts are identical in content,
1409	  reference resolution and activation.
1410	- **Multiple adapters:** the tools read each other's files (Codex and
1411	  OpenCode both read `AGENTS.md`; OpenCode also discovers `.claude/skills` and
1412	  `.agents/skills`), so with several adapters Belay plans one shared project
1413	  and writes each artifact once, where the tools find it:
1414	  - the **first adapter listed owns the one reference tree**, and every
1415	    adapter links into it;
1416	  - an instruction file several adapters place at one path (`AGENTS.md`) is
1417	    **written once**, by the first of them listed;
1418	  - OpenCode **writes no copy of a skill** Claude Code or Codex already
1419	    writes where it discovers it, and links to theirs;
1420	  - a command's `x-` skill that OpenCode would discover is an error
1421	    (`cross-discovery-activation`) unless `opencode.json` hides it with a
1422	    skill permission (`"permission": {"skill": {"x-*": "deny"}}`; the last
1423	    matching pattern decides) or `crossDiscovery` is set;
1424	  - a skill OpenCode finds in two directories (all three adapters enabled)
1425	    is a `cross-target-discovery` warning, since nothing in the project can
1426	    stop it.
1427	
1428	  `crossDiscovery: separate` means each tool's tree is deployed apart: every
1429	  adapter writes its own complete tree, and incompatible writes to one path
1430	  are rejected (`output-collision`). The whole plan is still checked before
1431	  anything is written.
1432	- Generated links (from `@{...}` references) are relative to the file that
1433	  contains them and must point at planned outputs (`broken-reference-link`).
1434	  Markdown links you write in prose are text and are never checked.
1435	- Discovery metadata and body are emitted exactly once. Frontmatter is written
1436	  with a format-aware YAML or TOML encoder. Generated filenames and native
1437	  metadata are checked against the target's schema, and unsupported requested
1438	  capabilities are diagnosed before anything is written.

1502	## 12. Package management
1503	
1504	Packages are git repositories, managed as **vendored dependencies**. Installed
1505	packages are stored inside the project and committed to version control, and
1506	the tooling adds, updates, removes and inspects them. Nothing is fetched at
1507	compile time.
1508	
1509	- **Offering packages.** A repository declares packages with `piton-package`
1510	  anchors (`PitonPackage` from `@piton/packaging`: `name`, `root`,
1511	  `dependencies`). A package anchor can live anywhere in the specbase but must
1512	  be listed under `packages:` in `piton.config.pi`. A package's `root` is
1513	  relative to `piton.config.pi`, like the project's own root. **`packages:` is what the
1514	  repository offers to other projects; a project never installs its own
1515	  packages.** One repository can offer several packages, each with its own
1516	  root and dependencies.
1517	- **Names.** `name` is what the package installs under. It exists because it
1518	  can be kebab-case (`my-package`), which an anchor name can't. Left out, the
1519	  anchor's own name is used. **Package names are flat: no `/`.** Names like
1520	  `@piton/belay` are only for the packages bundled with the compiler.
1521	- **Dependencies.** `dependencies:` lists git URLs, each with an optional
1522	  `commit:`, `tag:` or `branch:` on an indented line beneath it (a dictionary
1523	  item right after the URL). **Only one pin per URL**; more is
1524	  `multiple-pins`. Without a pin, the latest commit on the default branch is
1525	  used. **Pins are strings**: `@piton/config` types them as strings, so
1526	  `tag: 1.0` stays `"1.0"`. Other pin diagnostics are `dangling-pin` and
1527	  `unknown-pin`.
1528	- **Picking packages.** A repository can offer several packages. You get all
1529	  of them unless you list the ones you want with `packages:` under the URL:
1530	  `packages: [ui-kit]`.
1531	- **Project and package dependencies are separate.** The project's apply only
1532	  to the project, and each package declares its own.
1533	- **No nested dependencies.** When two packages need the same package at
1534	  different versions, **the one with the newest commit wins** and a warning is
1535	  shown.
1536	- **Installation.** Each package goes into `tethers/<name>`, next to
1537	  `piton.config.pi`, with the files from its `root`. A repository offering
1538	  `ui-kit` and `my-package` gives `tethers/ui-kit` and `tethers/my-package`.
1539	  Tethering removes every trace of git. A repository that offers no packages
1540	  is installed whole, under the name its URL implies.
1541	- **Importing.** An installed package is a location placeholder:
1542	  `from my-package import X`, `use my-package`, `use my-package/MyAnchor`.
1543	  Normal path resolution applies below it. A missing package is a compiler
1544	  error.
1545	- **Lock file.** `.piton/tether.lock`, next to `piton.config.pi`, keeps each
1546	  tethered package's URL, commit and a hash of its files. `tether` and
1547	  `update` write it, and it is committed with the project.
1548	- **Conflicts.** Before tether, update or any other operation on an installed
1549	  package, the tooling compares its files with the lock file and goes ahead
1550	  only if nothing changed. If the files were edited, it says so and asks the
1551	  user to untether (or `piton update --force` to discard the edits).
1552	
1553	The commands:
1554	
1555	- `piton tether` on its own installs everything in `dependencies`. Given a
1556	  source URL, it adds it to `dependencies` in `piton.config.pi` and installs
1557	  it. `--as <name>` installs under another name.
1558	- `piton update [packages...] [--force] [--diff]` reinstalls from
1559	  `dependencies`, all packages when none are named. `--force` replaces a
1560	  package even if it was edited, discarding the edits with a warning;
1561	  `--diff` prints a coloured unified diff of every file each update changed.
1562	- `piton untether <package>` moves the package from `tethers/` to
1563	  `<root>/untethered/` and rewrites the imports that named it, making it the
1564	  project's own source. `--as <name>` renames it; `--no-rewrite` only moves
1565	  it.
1566	- `piton remove <package>` deletes an installed package and removes it from
1567	  `dependencies`. It refuses if the files were edited or if anything still
1568	  imports the package.

1570	## 13. CLI reference
1571	
1572	Every command prints what it produced first, then a one-line outcome (✓ or
1573	✗), and its problems last: diagnostics, errors and warnings with their help
1574	and notes, then the error and warning count. On a terminal the output is
1575	coloured and paths are marked `+`/`-`; piped or with `NO_COLOR`, it is plain
1576	text and stdout carries the bare results.
1577	
1578	| Command | Behaviour |
1579	| --- | --- |
1580	| `piton check [paths...]` | Validates syntax, imports, references, types, inheritance, composition, exports and circular dependencies, reporting errors and warnings. Writes nothing. Exits 0 when there are no errors and 1 otherwise. Paths are optional files, directories or globs; the default is the project (or every `.pi` file under the working directory when there's no `piton.config.pi`). |
1581	| `piton build [config] [--dry-run]` | Builds the project configured by `piton.config.pi` (or the given config). Writes renderer output to `<output>/<path under root>.<ext>` (defaults: `./dist`, JSON), so `spec/components/Button.pi` becomes `dist/components/Button.json`: the entry file plus every file holding something the entry's exports reference. A registered framework's output replaces it unless the config sets `output` or `renderer`, which asks for both. Records every file in `.piton/manifest.json`. The whole plan is validated before anything is written. `--dry-run` reports without writing. |
1582	| `piton compile <path> [--renderer json\|yaml\|markdown] [--write] [--dependencies]` | Compiles one file to stdout (JSON by default): one key per export. `--write` writes `<file>.<ext>` next to each input and is required for globs. `--dependencies` wraps the result as `{"value": "<compiled output as a string>", "dependencies": [absolute source paths]}` so build tools know what to watch; bundled package files are left out. |
1583	| `piton format [path] [--check]` | Applies canonical formatting (4-space indents, constraint spacing, sorted and wrapped imports, no `.pi` in import paths, a space after `//`). `--check` reports without writing. `piton format -` reads source from stdin and writes the formatted text to stdout. It **only splits overflowing lines and never rejoins a paragraph**, so rewrap edited prose by hand, and don't reflow `key: value` blocks as prose. |
1584	| `piton reach [targets...] [--no-unreachable] [--no-paths]` | Starting from files, globs or anchor names (the entry by default), follows outgoing imports, references, inheritance and composition, direct and transitive. Reports what is reachable with its depth and the path taken, and what is unreachable. The flags hide the last two. Use it to find dead spec. Grouped by source, with a summary. No diagnostics; always exits 0. |
1585	| `piton slice <target> [--adapter <target>]` | Prints the part of the spec one thing depends on, as one Markdown document for an agent's prompt. The target is `file.pi#Anchor`, `file.pi#Anchor.property`, `file.pi#variable`, or a bare name looked up across the project (an error when more than one file declares it). Follows, transitively: what an anchor extends, every base that also declares a property, anchors named by type constraints, what a value read (`${Other.x}`, variables), and what it references or embeds. Imports alone bring nothing in. A whole anchor needs all its properties and bases; slicing a property leaves out the anchor's other properties; a reference to a property needs only that property. It also includes the **chain** from the project's entry down to the target (`Specification.Tooling`, `Tooling.cli`, `Cli.commands`): the shortest path the build takes, each link only that one property and not followed further. An export of the entry, a variable, and a file the build doesn't reach have no chain. Order: the target, then its dependencies nearest first (source order breaks ties), then the chain outermost first, so the same source prints the same bytes. Each declaration appears once, headed by its name as written (`SaveButton.color`), with its file, what it extends, its type and what it reads. References and embeds are written as names; cycles are followed until they come back around. Every path it prints is relative to the directory it runs in, and it finds the project by looking upward for `piton.config.pi`. `--adapter claude-code` (any Belay target the project builds) cites the compiled output instead: each location and every reference links to where `piton build` writes it (an embedded anchor to the section that embeds it), and no `.pi` file is ever cited; an abstract base or an anchor that is only read has no document of its own and is described without one. With `--adapter` the target itself must be something the build writes out. Markdown links the author wrote pass through unchanged. Exits 1 on errors. |
1586	| `piton init [directory] [--template <group/name>] [--adapter <id>...] [--list]` | Starts a new project from a template compiled into the compiler (no network needed). Templates come in groups: `piton/minimal` (plain Piton to JSON), `piton/library` (a package others can tether), `belay/application` (a shape instruction placed in `src/`, a skill, an agent and a command) and `belay/minimal` (the Belay config and one skill). Without a directory it first asks for the project's name and creates that directory (an empty answer, or no terminal, uses the working one). Then it asks for a group and a template (`--template belay` asks only for the template), and for a Belay template, which adapters to build for: a checklist of Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode with the template's default (Claude Code) checked, or `--adapter`, repeated or comma-separated. The chosen adapters replace the config's import and `adapters` list, and a template's `.adapters/<id>/` files (like OpenCode's `opencode.json`) are written only for the adapters chosen. Templates are the `group/name` directories in the compiler repo's `create-templates/`, each with a one-line `.template` description that is not written out; adding one is adding a directory, and every template must check cleanly, be formatted, and build. `--list` describes the groups and templates and does nothing else. With no terminal, a full template name is required. It never overwrites a file: if any it would write exists, it names each and writes none, and cancelling a question writes nothing. Prints each written path on stdout, then a summary and the next commands on stderr. Exits 1 on errors. |
1587	| `piton loc [paths...]` | Counts total, code, comment and blank lines per file, with a summary. Defaults to the project. No diagnostics; always exits 0. |
1588	| `piton lsp` | Runs the language server over stdio (section 14). |
1589	| `piton agent [claude] [--print-fluency] [args...]` | Launches the agent with a short project primer plus this fluency prompt (the project's `FLUENCY_PROMPT.md`, or the copy built into the compiler), passed to `claude` as `--append-system-prompt`. Extra arguments go to the agent. `--print-fluency` prints the prompt and does nothing else. |
1590	| `piton tether [source] [--as name]` | See section 12. |
1591	| `piton update [packages...] [--force] [--diff]` | See section 12. |
1592	| `piton untether <package> [--as name] [--no-rewrite]` | See section 12. |
1593	| `piton remove <package>` | See section 12. |
1594	
1595	Each CLI command in the spec is a `cli-command` anchor
1596	(`spec/scope/tooling/cli/index.pi`) with `commandName`, `positionalArguments`
1597	and `namedArguments`.
1598	
1599	## 14. Language server, editors, and JavaScript
1600	
1601	`piton lsp` provides, from the spec's feature list:
1602	
1603	- Diagnostics (not for missing optional properties), completion, hover (type,
1604	  source, documentation, inheritance chain, export status and compiled
1605	  interpretation), go-to-definition, find-references, and rename across the
1606	  whole specbase.
1607	- Auto-import, import organization, and code actions: import a missing
1608	  symbol, create an unresolved anchor, add an export, qualify an ambiguous
1609	  reference, resolve a simple inheritance conflict.
1610	- Document and workspace symbols, semantic highlighting, inlay hints
1611	  (resolved types, inherited origins, composition sources), formatting,
1612	  folding and selection ranges.
1613	- Inheritance, composition (`+`, `++`), override and conflict resolution;
1614	  reference resolution; validation and type information for expressions in
1615	  `{}`, `${}`, `#{}` and `@{}`; export validation; module resolution; cycle
1616	  detection (circular imports are fine and not reported).
1617	- Related-symbol navigation, a hierarchy view, resolved-value and provenance
1618	  inspection, compiled-output preview, source-to-output mapping, unused and
1619	  redundant definition detection, and documentation integration.
1620	- Incremental analysis and workspace indexing.
1621	- Diagnostics cover Belay semantics as well as Piton. Import organization
1622	  flags unused, duplicate, invalid and overly broad imports. Cycle detection
1623	  also catches an anchor that ends up extending itself, and shows the cycle.
1624	
1625	There is no signature help.
1626	
1627	Completion rules: never suggest things that don't exist; offer nothing on an
1628	empty value (`property: `), because prose probably follows; offer nothing
1629	after a `.` inside a string.
1630	
1631	Editing rules every editor must follow, through the LSP or the editor
1632	extension:
1633	
1634	- Enter after a colon that opens a dictionary or anchor property starts a new
1635	  line indented one level deeper.
1636	- Enter on a blank line inside a dictionary or anchor starts a new line one
1637	  level shallower.
1638	- Format-on-save is optional. It adds the space after `//` and touches nothing
1639	  else that is commented.
1640	
1641	Supported editors and their highlighters (spec): VS Code (TextMate plus LSP);
1642	Emacs, Helix and Zed (tree-sitter plus LSP); Neovim and Vim (vim syntax);
1643	JetBrains (`jetbrains`); Sublime (sublime-syntax); Kate (KSyntaxHighlighting).
1644	Every editor gets full LSP support. The integrations live under `editors/`.
1645	
1646	**Consuming Piton from JavaScript.** `packages/vite-plugin-piton` imports
1647	`.pi` files as modules, with HMR, dependency tracking (through
1648	`piton compile --dependencies`) and virtual modules. Each export in the Piton
1649	file is a named export, and the default export is the whole file, the same as
1650	`piton compile` gives:
1651	
1652	```ts
1653	import { SaveButton } from '../spec/app.pi';
1654	import spec from '../spec/app.pi';
1655	
1656	const button = SaveButton;
1657	const cancel = spec.CancelButton;
1658	```
1659	
1660	It has a configurable default renderer (`renderer: 'json' | 'yaml' |
1661	'markdown'`), and the renderers can also be imported as functions
1662	(`vite-plugin-piton/renderers`) and used inline. `packages/astro-piton` is an
1663	Astro integration that wraps the Vite plugin.

1666	
1667	1. **Orient.** Open `piton.config.pi` to find `root`, `entry`, `output`, the
1668	   frameworks, the adapters, `codeRoot` and `shapeRoot`. Read the entry file,
1669	   usually `spec/index.pi`, because its exports are the compilation roots.
1670	   Follow the `index.pi` files down through the modules. In this repository,
1671	   `spec/index.pi` exports `Specification` (FoundingThesis, Language, Tooling,
1672	   Belay, PackageManagement) plus the skills and command in `spec/agent/`.
1673	2. **Read compiled reference for overview, and source for truth.**
1674	   `<referenceRoot>/**/*.md` is easy to browse, and its links are lazy, so
1675	   follow them only when relevant.
1676	3. **Edit the `.pi` source**, following the conventions around it:
1677	   - one exported anchor per file, named after the file;
1678	   - `index.pi` files that re-export with `from ./X export *`;
1679	   - abstract anchors exported with a keyword, and shared abstracts in a
1680	     `lib/` folder;
1681	   - lowerCamelCase property names;
1682	   - SCREAMING_CASE for exported constant lists;
1683	   - prose in string blocks, and structure in keys and lists;
1684	   - `@{X}` to link related documents;
1685	   - examples inside fences wrapped in a `\\\` escape block.
1686	4. **Keep imports honest.** Use `use` for keywords and `from ... import` for
1687	   names; a file often needs both. A new file only compiles if the entry
1688	   reaches it, so export it through an index or reference it.
1689	5. **Validate.**
1690	   - Run `piton check`.
1691	   - `piton check` does **not** compile the examples inside escape blocks
1692	     (they are literal text). When you edit spec examples, extract each ` ```piton ` block,
1693	     run `piton compile` on it, and compare with any ` ```json ` block that
1694	     follows. Remember that compile output has only exported names.
1695	   - Run `piton build`, then look at the diff of the generated files.
1696	   - Run `piton reach` to confirm new anchors are reached.
1697	   - Run `piton format --check`.
1698	6. **Never hand-edit generated files.** That includes `CLAUDE.md` and
1699	   `AGENTS.md` under `codeRoot`, everything under `.claude/`, `.codex/`,
1700	   `.agents/`, `.opencode/` and the build output directory that is listed in
1701	   `.piton/manifest.json`, and the files in `.piton/` themselves.
1702	7. **Keep implementation and spec in agreement.** The implementation is judged
1703	   against the spec. When they disagree, report it instead of quietly bending
1704	   the spec to fit. Trust `piton compile` for how things behave today, and
1705	   flag the gap.
1706	
1707	## 16. Where the compiler differs from the spec
1708	
1709	Checked with `piton compile` and `piton build`:
1710	
1711	- The CLI has a few things the spec doesn't name: `build --dry-run`,
1712	  `tether --as`, agent argument passthrough, the `reach` flags, and
1713	  `format` with no path or `-`.
1714	
1715	- **Paragraph breaks.** The spec says a blank line in a string block starts a
1716	  new paragraph. The compiler joins the paragraphs with a single `\n`, which
1717	  Markdown output renders as one paragraph with a soft line break.
1718	
1719	Known limitations, where the spec is silent and the compiler's choice may
1720	surprise you:
1721	
1722	- A `/`-rooted import inside an installed package resolves against the
1723	  consuming project's root, not the package's. Use relative imports inside a
1724	  package.
1725	- A required property from an abstract is not satisfied by a value inherited
1726	  from a concrete base (`needs Thing extends Base`, where `Base` supplies it):
1727	  the keyword's anchor comes last, and its value-less declaration wins. Give
1728	  the value on the anchor itself.
1729	- `piton check` with no paths checks what the entry reaches, so a file that
1730	  nothing imports is not checked. Name it: `piton check path/to/file.pi`.
1731	- **Prose directly in an anchor body is silently dropped.** `anchor A:` with
1732	  only a line of text under it (no key) compiles to an empty anchor, with no
1733	  diagnostic. Always put prose under a key, such as `description:`.
1734	- Mixed-type equality is simply unequal: `{1 == "1"}` is `false`, not an
1735	  error. The spec says `==` works on every type but doesn't spell this out.
1736	- Which constructs each adapter requires a `description` for (section 11.2)
1737	  is hardcoded in `crates/piton-belay/src/adapter.rs`, not declared in the
1738	  adapter `.pi` files.
